title: Mein Ingeborg Bachmann Studium - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A personal literary reflection in which Cowen praises Ingeborg Bachmann's 1971 novel Malina and her letters with Max Frisch as among the best he has read, with no market or policy content.

insights.claim: Cowen rates Ingeborg Bachmann's 1971 Austrian novel Malina as deeper and more enjoyable than any of the famous 19th-century Victorian novels written by women, though he found it read less well in English translation.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: No direct investment relevance; a cultural/literary aside consistent with Cowen's recurring book-recommendation content.
insights.quote: I was pretty stunned by how good it was (it seems less good in English), and I would say I enjoyed it more, and found it deeper, than any of the famous 19th century Victorian novels by women.

insights.claim: Cowen calls the published letters between Ingeborg Bachmann and Max Frisch ("Wir haben es nicht gut gemacht") the best "letters book" he knows, noting an English translation is due out in November of the same year.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Signals a niche literary release (English translation of the Bachmann-Frisch letters) that may draw attention among literary-fiction readers and small publishers this fall.
insights.quote: It is called "Wir haben es nicht gut gemacht." Der Briefwechsel.

insights.claim: Cowen mentions a new 2026 Bachmann biography by Dieter Burdorf ("Dieses unruhige Ich: Ingeborg Bachmann") and other adaptations (a film and opera of Malina, a Bachmann-Frisch biopic) as part of a wider renewed interest in her work.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: No market relevance; purely cultural/biographical detail.
